patient.chief_complaint: Progressive memory difficulties and episodes of disorientation over the past 12 months
patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. Chen Wei is a 62-year-old right-handed retired schoolteacher who presents to the neurology outpatient clinic accompanied by her husband for evaluation of progressive memory difficulties over the past 12 months. Her husband first noticed changes approximately one year ago when she began misplacing everyday items such as her keys and reading glasses with increasing frequency. Over the subsequent months, she started forgetting recent conversations, sometimes asking the same questions multiple times within an hour. Approximately six months ago, she had an episode of becoming disoriented while walking in their neighborhood of 20 years, briefly unable to find her way home from the local market, which alarmed both patient and family. She has had several instances of leaving the stove on after cooking and forgetting to take her medications unless reminded. Her husband reports she has become less engaged in social activities and recently withdrew from her weekly mahjong group, citing difficulty keeping track of the tiles and game strategy. She has also had intermittent episodes of dizziness described as lightheadedness, particularly with position changes, which she attributes to her blood pressure medication. Of note, she occasionally reports vivid, brief dream-like images when falling asleep, describing scenes of people she does not recognize appearing in her bedroom doorway, though she recognizes these as not real. Her husband notes that her alertness and engagement seem to fluctuate throughout the day, with periods of being quite sharp alternating with periods of seeming 'foggy' or staring into space, though these fluctuations have been mild. She denies any falls, gait difficulties, tremor, hallucinations during full wakefulness, or loss of consciousness. She has not experienced any sudden neurological deficits, headaches, seizures, or changes in personality. She reports her mood has been somewhat low given her frustration with the memory problems, though she denies hopelessness, anhedonia, or suicidal ideation. She continues to perform basic activities of daily living independently but requires increasing assistance with managing finances and scheduling appointments.

clinical_assessment.impression: Cognitive impairment documented on a validated bedside instrument with an amnestic-predominant profile, and delayed recall that does not recover with cueing — a storage rather than a retrieval deficit, which is the pattern of Alzheimer pathology. Instrumental independence is preserved, so the syndrome is staged as mild cognitive impairment and not as dementia — the threshold is functional, and this assessment is where it is decided. This assessment is the step that makes the syndrome measurable; imaging and biomarkers then attribute it.

results.title: Lecanemab in Early Alzheimer's Disease - CLARITY AD 18-Month Extension
results.finding: Lecanemab continued to show reduced decline on CDR-SB vs placebo over 18 months of open-label extension. Greatest benefit in early-stage (MCI/mild AD) patients with confirmed amyloid pathology.

results.title: AAN Practice Guideline: Mild Cognitive Impairment Due to Alzheimer's Disease
results.finding: Recommends cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) as first-line symptomatic treatment. Memantine may be added at moderate stage. Emphasizes non-pharmacological interventions including cognitive stimulation, physical exercise, and caregiver support.

results.title: Aducanumab and Lecanemab: Disease-Modifying Anti-Amyloid Therapies for Alzheimer's Disease
results.finding: Anti-amyloid antibodies show modest but statistically significant slowing of cognitive decline in early AD. Require confirmation of amyloid pathology before initiation. ARIA (amyloid-related imaging abnormalities) is the main safety concern, occurring in 12-35% of patients.

output.summary: Cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) have demonstrated modest symptomatic benefits in mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease in randomized controlled trials. Disease-modifying anti-amyloid antibodies (lecanemab) showed statistically significant slowing of cognitive decline in early amyloid-confirmed AD, with effect sizes of approximately 27% reduction in CDR-SB progression, but carry risk of amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA) in 12–35% of patients. Non-pharmacological interventions including cognitive stimulation, physical exercise, and social engagement have shown supportive evidence.

useless_tools.rationale: ECG is unrelated to the dementia workup; no cardiac symptom or syncope to justify it in this case
Echocardiography is unrelated to the dementia workup; no cardioembolic indication in this presentation

sequence_constraints.reason: Obtain structural imaging before lumbar puncture to exclude mass effect / herniation risk, particularly in older patients

critical_actions: Obtain collateral history from an informant who knows the patient well
Exclude reversible causes of cognitive decline with screening labs (CBC, CMP, TSH, B12, folate; HIV/RPR per risk)
Obtain structural brain MRI with dementia/volumetric protocol
Quantify cognitive impairment with a standardized cognitive battery (MoCA at minimum; formal neuropsychological testing when feasible)
Assess safety: driving, medication management, finances, and need for caregiver support
Disclose the diagnosis and discuss prognosis, advance directives, and treatment options with the patient and family
Pursue biomarker confirmation (CSF AT(N) markers or amyloid PET) when MRI is equivocal or when an atypical AD variant is suspected
contraindicated_actions: Do not prescribe anticholinergic medications (e.g., diphenhydramine, oxybutynin, tricyclics) which worsen cognition in patients with AD
Do not prescribe benzodiazepines as first-line management of anxiety or insomnia given fall and cognitive risk
Do not start antipsychotics without a clear behavioral indication given the FDA boxed warning for increased mortality in dementia
Do not attribute symptoms entirely to normal aging, depression, or sleep apnea without completing the dementia workup
Do not start memantine monotherapy at the mild stage (memantine is approved for moderate-to-severe AD)
key_reasoning_points: MMSE may remain within the 'normal' range in highly educated patients with early AD; MoCA and formal neuropsychological testing are more sensitive at the MCI / mild dementia interface
The hallmark cognitive feature of AD is impaired delayed recall with rapid forgetting and limited benefit from cueing, reflecting a storage-type (hippocampal) memory deficit
APOE genotyping is a risk modifier and is not used to make the diagnosis; an E3/E4 or E4/E4 result is supportive but neither sufficient nor required for diagnosis
Low-normal B12 should prompt methylmalonic acid testing before being dismissed as a non-contributor
Cholinesterase inhibitors are first-line symptomatic therapy in mild-to-moderate AD; memantine is reserved for moderate-to-severe disease
